title: Decorators and context managers
subtitle: Add behaviour to any function, and guarantee cleanup
goal: Write decorators (with and without arguments) using functools.wraps, and build context managers with classes and contextlib.
outcomes: Explain a decorator as a function that returns a wrapper, using closures
Write logging and timing decorators that work on any function
Write decorators with arguments, like retry and permission checks

slides.title: Mission 29: Decorators and context managers
slides.body:
You have already used `@property`, `@lru_cache` and `with open(...)`. Today you build your own.

- **Decorators** add behaviour (logging, timing, retries, permissions) to any function without touching its code
- **Context managers** guarantee setup and cleanup around a block

left.title: Copy-pasted in every function
left.code:
def fetch_scores():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    ...
    print("took", time.perf_counter() - start)

def build_report():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    ...

visual.verdict: A decorator keeps cross-cutting code in one place.

slides.say: You have already used at property, at lru cache, and with open. Today you learn how they work, and you build your own. Decorators add behaviour like logging, timing, retries and permission checks to any function, without touching its code. Context managers guarantee that setup and cleanup happen around a block of code, even when something goes wrong.

slides.title: Function in, function out
slides.body:
A **decorator** is a function that takes a function and returns a new one, usually a `wrapper` that does something extra and calls the original.

It relies on yesterday's closures: the wrapper **remembers** the original function.
slides.say: A decorator is simply a function that takes a function and returns a new function. Usually the new one is a wrapper that does something extra, then calls the original. It works because of yesterday's closures. The wrapper remembers the original function it was given, so after decorating, the name greet points at the wrapper, and the wrapper still knows the real greet.

slides.title: A decorator by hand
explain: shout takes a function...
...defines a wrapper that calls it and changes the result...
...and returns the wrapper.
Decorating by hand: the name greet now points at the wrapper.
@shout above a def does exactly the same thing, automatically.
slides.say: Shout takes a function, builds a wrapper that calls it and shouts the result, and returns the wrapper. First we decorate by hand: greet equals shout of greet. Now the name greet points at the wrapper. The at sign syntax does exactly the same thing for us, right where the function is defined. That is all a decorator is.

slides.title: The @ line, and wrappers that fit any function
slides.body:
`@timer` above `def report(...)` is shorthand for `report = timer(report)`.

To wrap **any** function, whatever its arguments, the wrapper accepts `*args, **kwargs` (Day 18) and passes them straight through. And it must **return** the result.

visual.verdict: Identical result. The @ form keeps the decoration next to the definition.

slides.say: The at timer line above a function is shorthand for report equals timer of report. To make one decorator fit any function, whatever its parameters, the wrapper accepts star args and double star kwargs, which you met on day eighteen, and passes them straight through to the original. And it must return the original's result, or the caller gets None.

slides.title: A logging decorator
slides.body: One decorator, two very different functions. Debugging a big app often starts with exactly this.
explain: Accept any positional and keyword arguments.
Do something before the call.
Call the original with exactly the same arguments.
Hand the result back to the caller.
Every call now logs itself, with no change inside gst.
slides.say: This logging decorator works on any function. The wrapper accepts any arguments, logs the call, passes everything through to the original, logs the result and returns it. We apply it to a GST calculator and a greeting function, which take completely different arguments. Debugging a large app often starts with a decorator just like this.

slides.title: What happens on a decorated call
slides.body: Calling `gst(1000)` really calls `wrapper(1000)`, which calls the original `gst`. The original's result travels back up through the wrapper.
slides.say: Here is the call stack when you call gst of a thousand. The name gst points at the wrapper, so the wrapper runs first, with the arguments packed into args. The wrapper calls the original function, which returns a hundred and eighty. The result travels back up through the wrapper, which returns it to main.

slides.title: Predict the output
options:
start
registering hello
hello!
registering hello
slides.why: The decorator runs **once, when the def runs**, not on each call. `register` returns the function unchanged, so calling `hello()` just says hello. Web frameworks like Flask register their URL routes this way.
slides.say: This decorator prints a message and returns the function unchanged. When does that message appear: when the function is defined, or when it is called? Predict the order.

slides.title: functools.wraps
slides.body:
A plain wrapper hides the original: `report.__name__` becomes `"wrapper"` and the docstring is lost. Logs, tracebacks and tools all get confused.

Decorate your wrapper with `@functools.wraps(func)` to copy the name, docstring and more. Always do it.

visual.verdict: wraps keeps the decorated function honest about who it is.

slides.say: There is a catch with plain wrappers. After decorating, the function's name becomes wrapper, and its docstring disappears. Logs, tracebacks and documentation tools all get confused. The fix is one line: decorate your wrapper with functools dot wraps, passing the original function. It copies the name, the docstring and more. Professionals always do this.

slides.title: A timer decorator
slides.code:
import time
from functools import wraps


def timer(func):
    @wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
        print(f"{func.__name__} took {elapsed:.1f}s")
        return result
    return wrapper


@timer
def generate_report(rows):
    """Build the monthly sales report."""
    time.sleep(0.2)  # pretend this is slow work
    return f"Report with {rows} rows"


print(generate_report(500))
print(generate_report.__name__, "|", generate_report.__doc__)
slides.expect:
generate_report took 0.2s
Report with 500 rows
generate_report | Build the monthly sales report.
explain: @wraps(func) copies the name and docstring onto the wrapper.
Start a precise stopwatch.
How long did the real work take?
Return the result, so the caller gets it as usual.
Thanks to wraps, the name and docstring survive.
slides.say: Here is a real timing decorator. It starts a stopwatch, calls the function, measures how long it took, prints it and returns the result. Notice at wraps on the wrapper. Thanks to it, the decorated function still reports its true name and docstring. Put at timer on any slow function and you know exactly where your time goes.

slides.title: Decorators with arguments
slides.body: `@retry(times=3)` has brackets, so `retry(times=3)` runs **first** and must return the actual decorator. That means three layers of functions.

items: retry(times=3) runs, remembers times, returns decorator
fetch_score() calls wrapper, which tries up to 3 times

slides.say: Some decorators take settings, like retry three times. Because there are brackets, retry with times equals three runs first, and it must return the actual decorator. That decorator receives your function and returns the wrapper. So there are three layers: the settings, the decorator, and the wrapper. It looks like a lot of nesting, but each layer has one clear job.

slides.title: A retry decorator for flaky APIs
slides.body: Networks fail. A live-score API that is busy for a moment should not crash your app. This one fails twice, then succeeds.
slides.expect:
Attempt 1 failed: server busy
Attempt 2 failed: server busy
IND 287/4
explain: Layer 1: receives the setting and remembers it.
Layer 2: receives the function.
Layer 3: the wrapper that runs on every call.
Success: return immediately, no more attempts.
Every attempt failed: raise a clear error.
Our fake API fails on the first two calls.
slides.say: Networks fail all the time, and a cricket score API that is busy for a moment should not crash your app. Retry takes the number of attempts, the decorator takes the function, and the wrapper loops. Each failure is printed, a success returns at once, and if every attempt fails, it raises a clear error. Our pretend API fails twice, then returns the score.

slides.title: Quick check
options: The final result of the function
A decorator: a function that takes a function
slides.why: Python first evaluates `retry(times=3)`, then uses whatever it returns as the decorator. So it must return a function that accepts `func` and returns the wrapper.
slides.say: Quick check. When Python sees at retry with times equals three, it calls retry first. What must that call return?

slides.title: Context managers: the with protocol
slides.body:
`with` works with any object that has two methods:

- `__enter__()`: runs at the start; its return value goes to `as`
- `__exit__(exc_type, exc, tb)`: runs at the end, **always**, even after an error. It receives the error, if any. Return True to swallow it.
slides.say: The with statement works with any object that has two special methods. Dunder enter runs at the start, and whatever it returns goes into the name after as. Dunder exit runs at the end, always, even if the block raised an error, and it receives that error. If dunder exit returns True, the error is swallowed. That is how files close themselves.

slides.title: A transaction that rolls back
slides.body: Databases work like this: either **every** change in the block happens, or **none** does.
slides.code:
class Transaction:
    def __init__(self, wallet):
        self.wallet = wallet

    def __enter__(self):
        self.backup = dict(self.wallet)
        return self.wallet

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        if exc_type is not None:
            self.wallet.clear()
            self.wallet.update(self.backup)
            print("Rolled back:", exc)
        return True  # we handled the error


wallet = {"riya": 500, "arjun": 100}
with Transaction(wallet) as w:
    w["riya"] -= 200
    w["arjun"] += 200
print(wallet)
with Transaction(wallet) as w:
    w["riya"] -= 300
    raise ConnectionError("network dropped mid-transfer")
print(wallet)
explain: Save a copy of the wallet before the block runs.
This becomes w in the with statement.
An error happened inside the block...
...so restore the backup.
Returning True swallows the error. Most context managers return nothing, so errors carry on.
Half a transfer, then a failure: Riya's 300 rupees come back.
slides.say: Here is how databases keep your money safe. Dunder enter saves a backup of the wallet. If the block finishes, nothing more is needed. If an error interrupts it halfway, dunder exit restores the backup, so the half finished transfer is undone. We return True to say the error is handled. Most context managers return nothing, which lets the error carry on.

slides.title: Predict the output
slides.why: The error stops the block, but `__exit__` **still runs** before the error leaves the `with`. It returns None, so the error is not swallowed and the outer `except` catches it. Cleanup first, then the error.
slides.say: The block divides by zero halfway through. Dunder exit returns nothing. In what order do open, inside, close and caught appear?

slides.title: @contextmanager: the quick way
slides.body: `contextlib.contextmanager` turns a **generator** into a context manager: code before `yield` is the setup, code after it is the cleanup. Put the cleanup in `finally` so it runs even on errors. Test suites use this to change settings temporarily.
explain: The decorator turns this generator into a context manager.
Setup: apply the temporary changes.
yield hands control to the with block; the value goes to as.
finally: the cleanup runs even if the block raised.
The block fails, but the settings are still restored.
slides.say: Writing a class with two dunder methods is not always needed. Contextlib's contextmanager decorator turns a generator into a context manager. Everything before yield is setup, everything after is cleanup, and putting the cleanup in finally makes sure it runs even when the block fails. Test suites use exactly this to change settings temporarily.

slides.title: Fix the bug
slides.task: The decorator logs the call, but `add_gst(1000)` now returns **None** instead of 1180.0. Fix the wrapper.
slides.tests:
assert add_gst(1000) == 1180.0, "add_gst(1000) should still return 1180.0 after decorating. Does the wrapper return the result?"
@log_calls
def double(x):
    return x * 2
assert double(21) == 42, "Any decorated function should return its normal result."
assert "Calling add_gst" in __out__, "Keep the logging: the wrapper should still print Calling add_gst."
assert double.__name__ == "double", "Keep @wraps(func) so the name survives."
hints: The wrapper calls func, but what does it do with the answer?
slides.say: The most common decorator bug in the world. The logging works, but the decorated function now returns None. Remember what a wrapper must always do with the original function's result.

slides.title: A permission decorator
slides.task:
Web frameworks guard pages with decorators like `@login_required`. Write a decorator **with an argument**, `require_role(role)`.

The decorated function's first argument is a `user` dict. If `user["role"]` is not `role`, raise `PermissionError`. Otherwise call the function and return its result. Use `@wraps`.
hints: Three layers: require_role(role) returns decorator(func), which returns wrapper(user, *args, **kwargs).
In wrapper: if user["role"] != role, raise PermissionError(...).
Otherwise return func(user, *args, **kwargs). Put @wraps(func) above wrapper.
slides.say: Web frameworks protect pages with decorators. Write require role, a decorator that takes an argument. The wrapper checks the user's role, raises a permission error if it does not match, and otherwise calls the function and returns its result. You will need all three layers, and remember wraps.

slides.title: A Timer context manager
slides.task:
Write a class-based context manager `Timer`:

- `__enter__` records the start time with `time.perf_counter()` and returns `self`
- `__exit__` stores the seconds taken in `self.elapsed`, and must **not** swallow errors

Usage: `with Timer() as t: ...` then read `t.elapsed`.
slides.starter:
import time


class Timer:
    pass


with Timer() as t:
    time.sleep(0.1)
print(f"Took about {t.elapsed:.1f}s")
slides.solution:
import time


class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.start = time.perf_counter()
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        self.elapsed = time.perf_counter() - self.start
        return False


with Timer() as t:
    time.sleep(0.1)
print(f"Took about {t.elapsed:.1f}s")
slides.tests:
import time
with Timer() as t1:
    time.sleep(0.05)
assert isinstance(t1, Timer), "__enter__ should return self, so with Timer() as t gives you the Timer."
assert 0.04 <= t1.elapsed < 1, f"Sleeping 0.05s should give an elapsed time of about 0.05, got {t1.elapsed}."
t2 = Timer()
try:
    with t2:
        raise KeyError("boom")
    raise AssertionError("The KeyError disappeared. __exit__ must not swallow errors: return False or nothing.")
except KeyError:
    pass
assert hasattr(t2, "elapsed"), "elapsed should be set even when the block raises an error."
hints: __enter__(self): save time.perf_counter() in self.start and return self.
__exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb): set self.elapsed = time.perf_counter() - self.start.
Return False (or nothing) so errors are not swallowed.
slides.say: Build a timer you can wrap around any block of code. Dunder enter records the start time and returns the timer itself. Dunder exit stores the elapsed seconds. It must not swallow errors, and it must still record the time when the block fails. The tests check both.

slides.title: Mission 29 complete
points: A decorator takes a function and returns a wrapper; @deco means f = deco(f)
Wrappers accept *args, **kwargs, call the original, and return its result
Decorators with arguments need three layers: settings, decorator, wrapper
with calls __enter__, then __exit__ always, even after errors
slides.say: Mission twenty nine complete. You can write decorators that log, time, retry and guard functions, and context managers that guarantee cleanup, even when things go wrong. Tomorrow is project day: you will use everything from this phase to build a library management system with classes, files and JSON. See you on day thirty.
